articles.title: Where Numerology Began
articles.body:
People have attached meaning to numbers for a very long time, in many places.

Mesopotamia. The system used in this app is named after the Chaldeans, a people of ancient Babylonia who were known in the ancient world for astronomy and for reading the sky. The name 'Chaldean numerology' honours that reputation. Historians cannot show that the exact letter table used today was written in Babylon; the modern form was shaped much later, mostly in the last two centuries.

India. Indian traditions have long linked numbers with planets, days and names, and number symbolism appears in many classical texts.

Greece. Pythagoras and his followers, around 2,500 years ago, taught that number lies behind harmony and nature. Modern 'Pythagorean' numerology borrows his name, though its letter chart is also a later creation.

Hebrew tradition. Gematria gives each Hebrew letter a number and compares words by their totals.

Egypt and elsewhere. Many cultures used numbers symbolically in ritual and architecture.

The modern practice. What we call numerology today was gathered and popularised in Europe and America in the late 1800s and early 1900s, and it has kept evolving since.

A fair summary: the idea is ancient, the details are younger than they are often said to be, and the tradition is best treated as a belief system and a tool for reflection, not as a science.

articles.title: Chaldean vs Pythagorean
articles.body:
These are the two systems most people meet. They often give different numbers for the same name, so it helps to know which one you are looking at.

The letters. Pythagorean numerology runs the alphabet in order, 1 to 9, and repeats: A is 1, B is 2, and so on up to I which is 9, then J starts again at 1. Chaldean numerology uses only 1 to 8 and groups letters differently: A, I, J, Q, Y are 1; B, K, R are 2; C, G, L, S are 3; D, M, T are 4; E, H, N, X are 5; U, V, W are 6; O, Z are 7; F, P are 8.

The number 9. In the Chaldean table no letter is given the value 9. A total can still come to 9.

Compound numbers. Chaldean practice pays attention to the total before it is reduced, such as 15 or 26, as well as the single digit. Pythagorean practice usually goes straight to the single digit.

The name used. Chaldean readings usually work with the name you are actually known by, since that is the name people say and write. Pythagorean readings usually start from the full birth name.

Neither system can be proved right or wrong. They are two conventions. What matters is to use one consistently. This app uses the Chaldean system throughout.

articles.title: Why 9 Is Never Assigned to a Letter
articles.body:
Look at the Chaldean letter table and you will see the values run from 1 to 8. No letter is worth 9.

The traditional explanation is that 9 was regarded as a sacred or complete number, and so it was kept apart and not attached to any letter. This is the reason given by practitioners. It is a tradition, not a documented historical fact, and you will find it worded in slightly different ways.

There is a neat arithmetic property behind the feeling of completeness. Multiply 9 by any number and add the digits of the answer, and you come back to 9: 9 times 7 is 63, and 6 plus 3 is 9. Add 9 to any number and its reduced digit does not change: 5 plus 9 is 14, and 1 plus 4 is 5 again.

It is important to know that 9 still appears in results. A name can total 18 or 27, and both reduce to 9. A date of birth can reduce to 9 as well. The rule is only about the letter table.

articles.title: The Only Basics You Need
articles.body:
You can understand most of what this app shows with four ideas.

1. Name number. Give each letter of a name its Chaldean value and add them. For AMIET: A is 1, M is 4, I is 1, E is 5, T is 4, which makes 15.

2. Compound and single. The total, 15, is the compound number. Add its digits, 1 plus 5, to get the single number, 6. Chaldean readings look at both.

3. Birth number. Take the day of the month you were born and reduce it. Born on the 15th: 1 plus 5 is 6. Born on the 7th: it is simply 7.

4. Destiny number. Add every digit of the full date of birth. For 15 August 1990: 1+5+8+1+9+9+0 is 33, and 3 plus 3 is 6.

A few practical points.

Spelling matters, because changing a letter changes the total. That is why the app lets you compare two spellings.

Use the name you are really known by.

The short meanings in the app are general themes for each single number. They are a starting point for thinking, not a verdict on a person.

No number is good or bad on its own. A reading looks at how the numbers sit together.

articles.title: What a Consultation Can and Cannot Do
articles.body:
What it can do.

Look at your name number, birth number and destiny number together, including the compound numbers, which the quick check only shows briefly.

Compare spellings of a personal or business name and explain how each one changes the picture.

Give you a structured way to think about your tendencies, your choices and your timing, and questions worth asking yourself.

Leave you with a written summary you can return to.

What it cannot do.

It cannot predict events with certainty or guarantee an outcome.

It is not medical, legal, financial or psychological advice, and it should never replace a qualified professional.

It cannot make a decision for you. A change of spelling does not act on its own; what you do still matters most.

How to get the most from one.

Bring the exact spelling of the name you use and your full date of birth. Come with one or two real questions. Treat what you hear as a perspective to weigh, and keep what is useful.
